newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Henkel sets 96 records, eyes more in 97.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Henkel sets 96 records, eyes more in 97.

text.p: German chemicals group Henkel KGaA, fresh from announcing various acquisitions, on Monday said it expects to post more record results this year, as the new groups were seen contributing to results soon.
"We plan to have a higher net profit in 1997 than we did in 1996," Henkel chief executive Hans-Dietrich Winkhaus told a news conference after detailing record 1996 results.

Last year the Henkel group, best known for its Persil washing powder, posted a six percent rise in net profit to 515 million marks ($303.7 million) while sales shot 15 percent higher to 16.3 billion marks.

Shareholders also profited from the stronger results as the payout on common shares was raised by 14 percent to 1.20 marks and the dividend for preference shares was increased by 13 percent to 1.30 marks.
Henkel executives based their optimism for the full year on the first two months' performance where sales and profits across all divisions were above year-ago levels.

"We do expect another increase in 1997, particularly as earlier acquisitions like the Schwarzkopf takeover were integrated more quickly than expected and are already positive for the group," chief financial officer Ulrich Lehner told Reuters Financial Television.
On the other hand, Lehner also said Henkel now needed to digest some of the high-profile takeovers made last year and that other acquisitions might have to wait for a while.
"The major issue this year will be to integrate the acquisitions we have made," Lehner said.
Winkhaus added that the restructuring and integration efforts will cost the company quite a lot of money this year.
He said the takeover of U.S. adhesives group Loctite, a strategically important move for Henkel as it opens up the U.S. market for the group, would weigh on results this year.
Analysts had said Henkel has scored a strategic coup by acquiring the U.S. adhesives group in December but that the $1.3 billion price tag was very high.
Overall analysts said Henkel's strategy of expanding its global reach was paying off, particularly since domestic sales remained sluggish, falling three percent last year.
Acquisitions helped contribute 11 percent in total results, Henkel said.

Meanwhile Henkel pared back jobs at its main site by four percent to 9,000 workers and expects that more jobs will be lost this year. Personnel director Roland Schulz however declined to say how many more jobs might be eliminated.
Worldwide, Henkel cut its workforce to 47,000 from 50,000.
Henkel shares however fell nearly three percent in bourse trade to 90.80 marks as dealers said the figures, although good, were still below expectations.
